strengths: The paper identifies an important and realistic gap: unlearning requests for text-to-image diffusion models are likely to arrive sequentially, while most existing work assumes a batch setting.
The continual unlearning formulation is clear, with useful distinctions between unlearning accuracy, in-domain retention, and cross-domain retention.

The empirical diagnosis of rapid retention collapse for ConAbl and EraseDiff is compelling at a high level, and the comparison with simultaneous unlearning usefully exposes the efficiency-utility tradeoff.

The regularization perspective is sensible and leads to several practical add-on baselines, including L1/L2 update penalties, selective fine-tuning, model merging, and semantic-aware gradient projection.
The paper includes experiments across style and object unlearning and tests compatibility of the proposed gradient projection with other regularizers, which strengthens the empirical story.
weaknesses: The evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims. It relies almost entirely on UNLEARNCANVAS, a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion setting with 80 predefined concepts, templated prompts, and classifier-based metrics. This leaves open whether the conclusions hold for broader text-to-image models, realistic prompts, personal identities, copyrighted content, unsafe concepts, or modern foundation-scale pipelines.

The results are mostly presented as plots without sufficient numeric tables, confidence intervals, multiple random sequences, or statistical analysis. Since continual unlearning can be sensitive to request order, concept choice, seeds, and hyperparameters, this substantially weakens the evidence.

The proposed theoretical analysis is fairly generic: a Taylor/Lipschitz-style bound mainly restates that small parameter drift can limit loss change under smoothness assumptions. It does not tightly explain unlearning-specific behavior or justify why the proposed regularizers should preserve retention while maintaining erasure.

The semantic-aware gradient projection method is under-specified and somewhat mathematically unclear. The projection is described over text-embedding subspaces, but gradients for cross-attention matrices live in parameter space; the paper does not fully clarify the exact tensor operation or prove that the stated first-order invariance meaningfully preserves generated concepts.

The efficiency claims are incomplete. Model merging requires independently unlearning concepts from the pretrained model and then merging, which may not satisfy the online continual constraint in a practical deployment. Training costs, memory costs, and per-request latency are not reported in enough detail.

The baseline coverage is limited. Only two base unlearning methods are studied, and comparisons to continual-learning style methods, replay/preservation-data approaches, EWC/SI-like regularizers, LoRA/adapters, or recent concept-erasure methods are limited or absent.

The evaluation of unlearning success is not robust. Classifier-based UA may miss residual concept knowledge under paraphrased prompts, adversarial prompts, compositional prompts, or human perception; no attack-style or qualitative failure analysis is provided.

Reproducibility details are insufficient: exact request sequences, hyperparameters, auxiliary concept generation/filtering, compute budget, and implementation details for each add-on are not fully specified in the main paper.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant setting: unlearning requests for text-to-image models often arrive sequentially, and evaluating single-shot unlearning methods under this protocol is a useful contribution.
The benchmark protocol is reasonably clear and separates unlearning accuracy, in-domain retention, and cross-domain retention, which helps expose different failure modes.

The empirical observation that naive sequential application of ConAbl/EraseDiff causes rapid retention collapse is plausible and important, and the paper gives several intuitive mitigation baselines such as norm regularization, selective fine-tuning, model merging, and gradient projection.
The paper is generally readable and well organized, with helpful qualitative figures and an effort to connect observed degradation to parameter drift.
weaknesses: The contribution is not sufficiently strong for acceptance at a top-tier AI venue. Much of the proposed solution space consists of straightforward adaptations of existing continual learning, model merging, pruning, and gradient projection ideas, with limited algorithmic novelty.

The evaluation is too narrow to support the broad claims. Experiments appear centered on UNLEARNCANVAS with a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion checkpoint, a small fixed concept universe, template prompts, and classifier-based metrics. It is unclear whether the conclusions transfer to real-world copyright, identity, safety, or open-vocabulary unlearning requests.

The main metric setup is fragile: UA and RA depend on specialized classifiers rather than robust semantic or human evaluation, and the paper does not convincingly address generation quality, prompt diversity, adversarial rephrasing, partial leakage, or whether concepts are truly erased rather than merely avoiding classifier labels.

The theoretical analysis is weak. The Taylor-bound argument mostly formalizes the unsurprising fact that small parameter changes tend to preserve loss under smoothness assumptions; it does not establish that parameter drift is the causal mechanism of collapse or that the proposed regularizers are near-optimal.

The gradient projection method is under-specified and only lightly justified. The relationship between projecting gradients of cross-attention matrices and preserving semantically similar concepts is not developed rigorously enough, and the auxiliary concepts generated by an LLM introduce reproducibility and sensitivity concerns.

Baselines and ablations are incomplete. The paper does not sufficiently compare against stronger continual learning regularizers/replay-style methods, alternative unlearning schedules, hyperparameter-matched sequential baselines, or methods that store/reuse retained concept data.

Statistical reliability is unclear. The paper reports trends from random concept sequences and generated images, but does not provide enough evidence on variance across many sequences, seeds, prompts, or concept orderings.

Efficiency claims are only partially substantiated. Simultaneous unlearning is described as prohibitively expensive, but the computational costs, memory costs, and latency of model merging, auxiliary concept generation, and gradient projection are not analyzed in enough detail.
Reproducibility is limited: many implementation details, hyperparameters, concept sequences, LLM-generated auxiliary sets, and tuning procedures are not sufficiently specified in the main paper.
Overall, the paper raises a relevant problem and has some useful empirical observations, but the novelty, rigor, and breadth of evidence fall short of the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Introduces and clearly motivates continual unlearning for text-to-image diffusion models, a timely and practically important setting that is underexplored relative to one-shot or simultaneous unlearning.

Provides a coherent benchmark protocol using UNLEARNCANVAS, with distinct measurements for unlearning accuracy, in-domain retention, and cross-domain retention; this makes the collapse phenomenon easy to diagnose.

Empirically demonstrates a strong and useful finding: standard unlearning methods such as ConAbl and EraseDiff retain high unlearning accuracy but suffer rapid retention collapse under sequential requests.

The regularization perspective is compelling and practically useful: L1/L2 penalties, selective fine-tuning, model merging, and gradient projection are plug-in additions rather than fully new unlearning pipelines.
The semantic-aware gradient projection idea is well aligned with the observed failure mode and gives clear gains for in-domain retention, especially when combined with other regularizers.
The paper is generally well organized, with helpful figures and a good distinction between diagnostic results, generic regularization, and semantic-aware mitigation.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is still somewhat narrow: experiments appear centered on UNLEARNCANVAS and a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion checkpoint, so it is unclear how well the conclusions transfer to larger modern T2I systems, broader prompts, real user removal requests, or non-curated concepts.

The evaluation relies heavily on specialized classifiers and template prompts. This is convenient and standardized, but may not capture semantic leakage, adversarial prompting, perceptual image quality, memorized content removal, or human judgments of whether a concept has truly been erased.

The paper claims a first systematic study, but the baselines are limited mainly to ConAbl and EraseDiff plus add-ons. More recent diffusion unlearning methods, safety editing methods, or continual learning baselines would strengthen the positioning.

The theoretical analysis is mostly a plausibility argument: the Taylor bound essentially says retention loss can grow with parameter distance, but it does not tightly explain when unlearning succeeds, how drift interacts with specific diffusion layers, or why the proposed projection should preserve actual generated concepts beyond first-order local behavior.

Details needed for reproducibility are incomplete in the main paper, especially the exact hyperparameters, random sequence variability, auxiliary concept generation/filtering procedure for gradient projection, and compute/runtime tradeoffs among sequential, simultaneous, merging, and projection methods.

The results would be more convincing with statistical variability across multiple unlearning sequences and seeds; some key figures appear to show single trajectories, making robustness of the gains hard to judge.

The method may depend on text-embedding similarity as a proxy for concept interference, but this proxy can fail for polysemous concepts, multi-token styles/objects, rare names, or visual similarity not reflected in text embeddings.

Ethical and legal implications are discussed as motivation, but the paper does not deeply evaluate whether the proposed continual unlearning actually satisfies realistic deletion, copyright, privacy, or safety requirements.

strengths: Addresses an important and realistic gap: unlearning requests are sequential in practice, while most text-to-image unlearning work assumes a batch setting.
The paper is well motivated and clearly defines continual unlearning with separate unlearning, in-domain retention, and cross-domain retention metrics.
The empirical story is coherent: existing methods exhibit rapid retention collapse, parameter drift correlates with this collapse, and regularization-based add-ons improve retention.
Evaluation covers more than one unlearning method and setting, including ConAbl, SculpMem, celebrity erasure, and an SDXL/ESD appendix, which strengthens the generality of the observations.
The proposed semantic-aware gradient projection is a useful and compatible add-on, and the analysis connecting semantic similarity to collateral forgetting is intuitive and practically relevant.
The paper is generally readable, with helpful qualitative figures and a clear organization from problem setup to diagnosis to mitigation.
weaknesses: The main contribution is closer to a systematic empirical study plus regularization add-ons than a fundamentally new continual unlearning algorithm; novelty is solid but not especially deep.

The evaluation relies heavily on classifier-based metrics on UNLEARNCANVAS-style concepts. This may not fully capture semantic erasure, image quality, prompt diversity, or whether the concept can be recovered with stronger prompting.

The sampled unlearning sequences appear limited, and the paper does not clearly report variance over many random orders. Continual unlearning performance can be highly order-dependent, so stronger statistical evidence is needed.

The theoretical analysis is fairly weak: the Taylor/Lipschitz argument mainly formalizes that small parameter changes imply small local loss changes, but does not strongly explain why sequential unlearning drifts more or why the proposed regularizers should be optimal.

The gradient-projection method is under-specified in important details, including how auxiliary concepts are generated, filtered, how many are used, sensitivity to this choice, and the exact projection implementation for matrix-valued cross-attention gradients.

The work does not sufficiently evaluate robustness of unlearning against adversarial recovery, paraphrased prompts, prompt engineering, or alternative recognizers, which is important for claims about safe/accountable generative AI.

Some baselines and comparisons could be stronger in the main paper, especially against more recent preservation-aware or adversarial-preservation concept erasure methods rather than mostly ConAbl/SculpMem in the core results.
Reproducibility details such as hyperparameter selection, compute cost, seeds, code availability, and tuning fairness are not sufficiently explicit in the extracted manuscript.

strengths: The paper identifies a realistic and underexplored setting: unlearning requests for text-to-image diffusion models arriving sequentially rather than all at once.

The empirical diagnosis that sequential unlearning causes severe retention collapse is clear and useful, and the comparison to simultaneous/independent unlearning helps isolate cumulative parameter drift as a plausible contributor.
The paper evaluates multiple add-on mitigation strategies and includes some breadth beyond the main UnlearnCanvas setup, including SculpMem, celebrity erasure, and an SDXL/ESD appendix experiment.
The distinction between in-domain and cross-domain retention is a useful evaluation lens, and the semantic-similarity analysis motivates why retaining nearby concepts is harder.
weaknesses: The main methodological contribution is weakly novel: L1/L2 regularization, selective fine-tuning, model merging, and gradient projection are largely standard ideas adapted to this setting. The proposed semantic gradient projection is conceptually simple and not developed into a strong standalone continual unlearning algorithm.

The evaluation relies heavily on classifier-based UA/RA metrics on a benchmark with fixed concept vocabularies. This may not reflect perceptual image quality, partial concept leakage, prompt diversity, or true legal/privacy unlearning requirements.

The experimental protocol appears narrow: only short sequences of 12 styles/objects in the main benchmark and 6 celebrities in the appendix, with limited discussion of variance over request order, random seeds, concept difficulty, or statistically meaningful confidence intervals.

The paper does not adequately evaluate robustness of unlearning. There is no serious adversarial prompt/recovery analysis, memorization leakage test, or evaluation of whether concepts are actually removed rather than hidden from the chosen classifier.

The theoretical analysis is fairly superficial: bounding retention loss by parameter distance via a Taylor expansion mainly formalizes an intuition and does not tightly explain unlearning dynamics or justify the proposed methods beyond generic drift control.

Some claims are overstated. Calling this a principled solution or a robust foundation seems stronger than the evidence, especially since gradient projection is sometimes worse than model merging and mainly helps when combined with other regularizers.

Important implementation details are underspecified, including hyperparameter selection, auxiliary concept generation/filtering, tuning costs, and how methods are balanced for compute. This limits reproducibility and makes it hard to assess fairness of comparisons.

The paper lacks a convincing discussion of practical deployment constraints and ethics. Continual unlearning is motivated by safety/legal concerns, but the proposed evaluation does not establish compliance-grade removal or address failure modes from false confidence in unlearning.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and realistic gap in diffusion-model unlearning: requests often arrive sequentially, and the work gives a clear formulation of continual unlearning with unlearning accuracy, in-domain retention, and cross-domain retention metrics.
The empirical finding of rapid retention collapse under sequential unlearning is compelling and well motivated, with useful comparisons to simultaneous and independent unlearning strategies.

The regularization perspective is coherent: parameter drift analysis, L1/L2 penalties, selective fine-tuning, model merging, and semantic-aware gradient projection form a sensible suite of baselines and add-ons rather than an isolated trick.

The semantic-interference analysis is a strong part of the paper. The correlation between text-embedding similarity and retention degradation motivates the gradient-projection method, which appears to improve in-domain retention and combine well with other regularizers.
The appendices strengthen the case by including additional results for SculpMem, celebrity unlearning, and SDXL/ESD, suggesting the observed failure mode is not limited to one narrow implementation.
weaknesses: The main contribution is closer to a systematic empirical study plus add-on regularizers than a fundamentally new continual unlearning algorithm. Several components are adapted from known continual learning, selective fine-tuning, and model merging ideas, which limits novelty.

The evaluation relies heavily on classifier-based metrics from UnlearnCanvas. This is useful for standardization, but it may not fully capture true concept erasure, image quality, prompt generalization, or whether unlearned concepts can be recovered through adversarial or paraphrased prompts.

The theoretical analysis is mostly a loose Taylor-style justification that small parameter drift should help retention. It supports the intuition but does not tightly explain why simultaneous unlearning drifts less or why the proposed projection should preserve generation behavior beyond first-order embedding effects.

The benchmark setting is still relatively controlled: fixed concept sets, templated prompts, and a limited number of sequential requests. More diverse open-vocabulary prompts, longer request streams, and real user-style deletion requests would make the claims stronger.

The paper acknowledges robustness to adversarial recovery only as future work. For machine unlearning, especially in generative models, the absence of a stronger privacy/security evaluation leaves some uncertainty about whether high UA corresponds to meaningful erasure.

Reproducibility details are somewhat incomplete from the manuscript alone, especially hyperparameter selection, computational cost across all methods, auxiliary-concept generation details, and whether code/checkpoints will be released.
